current_sentence: \begin{abstract} Machine-learning-based intrusion detection in supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems is not only a classification problem; it is also a communication-budget problem. A detector must receive sufficient telemetry, complete record-level processing before the next operational decision point, and remain useful when measurements are missing or communication channels fail. We evaluate four lightweight detectors---Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and a compact multilayer perceptron---on the MSU/ORNL Power System Attack Dataset using leave-one-run-out evaluation across fifteen collection runs. We measure batch-size-one detector-pipeline latency, translate feature budgets into modeled payload bytes, test robustness to missing telemetry and relay-channel loss, and compare edge-visible with centrally aggregated telemetry conditions. Random splitting substantially overstated cross-run performance: Random Forest ROC-AUC decreased from 0.972 to 0.677 under run-aware evaluation. Logistic Regression, XGBoost, and the compact multilayer perceptron satisfied the 10~ms and 16.7~ms study reference budgets at P95, whereas Random Forest satisfied only the 100~ms operational budget. A training-fold-selected 16-feature configuration reduced modeled payload from 512 to 64 bytes per record while retaining competitive unseen-run discrimination. Central aggregation generally provided stronger discrimination than edge-visible telemetry, but relay loss could remove that advantage. The results show that low inference latency alone does not establish deployability: unseen-run discrimination, alert burden, telemetry availability, and placement must be evaluated jointly. \end{abstract}
